Mendeleev noticed that elements of very different atomic weights often had similar properties, sodium and potassium both bonded with one chlorine atom, magnesium and calcium both bonded with two, etc. At the time, new elements were being discovered frequently, and the more that were discovered and measured accurately, the more they fit the pattern. Of then there would be a missing element, but given the frequency in which new elements were discovered, it was not unreasonable to assume those missing elements existed. It is kind of like putting together a jigsaw puzzle. At first you only have a few pieces that fit together, but the more fragments you have, the clearer the picture becomes.

questions_and_answers.question: 🎈 It's the birthday of Dmitri Mendeleev, the father of the modern periodic table! 🔬 Dmitri Mendeleev was a chemist who revolutionized our understanding of how elements are organized. He is best known for creating the Periodic Table of Elements, which classifies elements by their atomic weight and properties in a systematic and predictive format. This tool has been fundamental in the development of modern chemistry and has aided scientists in predicting the discovery of new elements. 📊 Mendeleev's work on the Periodic Table began in the mid-1860s when he was writing a chemistry textbook and realized that there was a pattern to the way elements behaved. He noticed that when the elements were ordered by increasing atomic weight, certain types of chemical behavior repeated themselves. This led him to formulate the Periodic Law, which states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights. 🌐 By arranging the 63 known elements into a table, Mendeleev was able to not only classify the elements but also predict the properties of elements that had not yet been discovered. For example, he foresaw the existence and properties of germanium, gallium, and scandium, which were discovered later and fit perfectly into the gaps he had left in his table. 🎖️ Mendeleev's visionary work provided a clear, organized system that could be expanded upon as new elements were discovered.

questions_and_answers.answer: The periodic table was born from a game of chemical solitaire. In 1869, Dmitri Mendeleev wrote the known elements on cards, dealt them across his desk, and boldly left blank spaces. Before this breakthrough, chemistry was a chaotic discipline. Scientists had discovered about 60 elements, from ancient staples like gold and carbon to newer finds like barium and iodine. But no one knew how many elements were left to find, or if there was any underlying logic connecting them. It was like having a box of jigsaw puzzle pieces with no picture on the cover. Chemists desperately searched for patterns. In 1829, Johann Döbereiner noticed "triads" of similar elements, like chlorine, bromine, and iodine. In 1864, John Newlands proposed a "Law of Octaves," suggesting every eighth element had similar properties, much like musical notes. questions_and_answers.answer: Dmitri Mendeleev created and published the periodic table in 1869. At this time, Mendeleev was a chemistry teacher at the University of Saints Petersburg in Russia. He was a well known educator in chemistry and researcher in the same field. When Mendeleev came back from a conference in Germany, he decided to take all the known elements of the periodic table and write their properties on a card. It was there that he sorted these cards over and over again in order to discover a pattern. After waking up from a dream, he came to realize that the best way to organize these elements was by their atomic mass. Thus, he created his version of the periodic table using the atomic weights.
